beats.say: Three passes apiece. One test left to score. Each coding assistant gets one try. The permission test checks that a denied request stays blocked. A failed it. If B passes, would you switch?

One task passes for Model B. Its answer keeps the request blocked. B wins four to three. Five tasks ended in ties. If either assistant was equally likely to win that last task, how surprising is B's lead?

Take the permission task. An explicit denial must stay denied. We give each model the same prompt and hidden tests, then keep both outcomes on one row. Pairing by task preserves this shared difficulty. Related versions of one task would need a cluster-level analysis.

Here are all six rows. Model A passes three; Model B passes four. The observed lift is one extra pass divided by all six tasks. We keep the task population, checkpoint, decoding and attempt budget attached to that description.

Subtract A from B within each row. A shared pass and a shared failure each contribute zero. Only a disagreement changes the signed difference. The permission row contributes plus one; the five ties stay in the denominator of the overall lift.

Six tasks were our close-up. Finish the planned forty-task run before drawing a conclusion. These are illustrative outcomes, with the same one-attempt protocol throughout. Watch the original permission row join seven more B-only passes, while five tasks favor A.

Twenty-seven pairs agree. Eight favor B and five favor A. The net gain is three passes across forty tasks, or seven and a half percentage points. Before looking at these results, we chose a one-sided question: does B improve the pass rate?

For that directional test, the equal-win boundary gives A and B the same chance on a disagreement. Start with our permission row alone. Its two possible directions are equally likely. A single B win has a one-sided tail probability of one half.

Now keep all thirteen disagreement identities and assign each a fair direction under that model. The twenty-seven ties stay parked. Independent task pairs let us multiply the coin probabilities. One simulated row of signs produces one count of B wins.

Enumerating every possible sign assignment gives this binomial distribution. Every assignment is equally likely, but the middle counts occur in many more assignments. The height of a bar is the fraction of assignments with that many B wins.

Our observed count is eight B wins. Include eight, nine, and every larger count: each is at least as favorable to B. Add those bar probabilities. Under the equal-win model, this happens about twenty-nine percent of the time. This sample gives fairly ordinary results under that model.

That p-value is a tail probability for outcomes generated by the null model. A two-sided question would also count equally extreme A wins, shown on the other side. We choose the direction before seeing results. Here we retain the original one-sided plan and its full right tail.

A five-percent significance threshold defines a repeated-use rule. With thirteen disagreements, ten or more B wins trigger rejection. The colored studies are false positives when equal win chances really hold. Their exact long-run probability is a little below five percent because the counts are discrete.

Now specify a real advantage: B wins sixty-five percent of disagreements. Keep the same rejection rule. Some simulated studies detect the advantage; others miss it. Power is the probability of detection under this specified alternative. A missed rejection leaves the comparison unresolved.

Plan for sixty-four independent disagreements instead. The critical count changes to preserve the error limit, and more studies now detect the same advantage. The exact power rises to about seventy-one percent. These sample sizes count disagreements; a full task study must also allow for how often models tie.

Imagine repeating that thirteen-disagreement test for twenty prompt variants whose results are independent under this example. Even when every variant has equal win chances, a family gets twenty opportunities for a false positive. The exact per-test error compounds to about sixty-one percent for at least one.

Bonferroni spends the family error budget across all twenty comparisons. The smaller per-test threshold moves our rejection boundary from ten B wins to twelve. Only the farthest tail survives. The union bound keeps family error at most five percent even when comparisons depend on one another.

Repeated looks at one accumulating experiment create another search. This fixed null sequence crosses the nominal line once, then moves back above it. Stopping at the first crossing would select the favorable look. Fix the stopping rule in advance, use a valid sequential method, or keep a fresh set for the final comparison.

The tail answered a question about the null. To estimate the size of the lift, draw forty whole task rows with replacement from our observed forty. The permission row can appear again. Its A failure and B pass travel together, so every draw still has a paired difference.

Compute the mean difference for that resample, then repeat with the same row rule. These bars accumulate eight thousand resampled means. The original rows remain the source of every draw. We resample clusters instead when a family of related tasks shares randomness.

Leave the lowest and highest two and a half percent of these means outside. The remaining interval runs from about minus ten to plus twenty-five percentage points. It crosses zero. With a small sample of passes and failures, this percentile interval can miss the true lift more often than we'd like. How could we check how often it works?
B costs more to run. We set the gold line at two extra passes per hundred tasks. The dot is our gain of seven and a half points. Open the interval around it. Does its lower end clear the gold line?
Hold the switch. The low end is minus ten points. We could lose passes even though B came out ahead on these forty tasks. Freeze the chosen model and run both assistants on fresh tasks.

Before the fresh comparison, settle one more protocol choice: how many attempts does each task receive? For the permission task, here is a separate illustrative pool of ten independent candidates from one fixed model and decoding setup. Two pass. Choose three candidates without replacement. Will this highlighted subset contain a pass?

This subset contains a passing candidate. Move several other three-candidate subsets through the same test, keeping their identities. There are a hundred and twenty distinct subsets in total. Fifty-six contain only failures; sixty-four contain at least one pass. Each subset has the same selection probability.

The estimated pass at three is the fraction of subsets with a pass. The complement formula counts the all-failing subsets efficiently. This estimates the fixed model’s three-attempt success target under independent sampling. Keep the ten-candidate estimation pool and the three-attempt operating budget explicit. Our release comparison continues with one attempt for both models.

Try the decision rule on a new illustrative holdout, collected once after freezing B. It has four hundred fresh matched tasks, with the same hidden-test policy and one attempt per model. Keep these rows separate from the development set. Fifty-two favor B, twelve favor A, and the rest agree.

Subtract the A-only wins and divide by all four hundred tasks. The lift is ten percentage points. Resampling these whole paired rows gives this new approximate interval. Compare its lower endpoint with our original useful-lift threshold. Which action does the frozen rule call for?
The low end is plus six and a quarter points. With one try per task, even that end clears our two-point cutoff. Switch to B.
